```{r setup, include = FALSE}
has_deps <- requireNamespace("edgeR", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("limma", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = has_deps)
```

## The problem

In a case/control single-cell study, samples differ in how much ambient RNA
they carry. Fragile disease tissue lyses more, so its soup is larger and is
enriched for the disease genes of whichever cell type is abundant. Those
reads land in every droplet. A pseudobulk test on a rare cell type then
reports the abundant type's disease genes as differentially expressed in the
rare type.

`ambient_de()` does not subtract the soup. It puts each sample's measured
soup inside the model as a known additive term:

$$y_{gs} \sim \mathrm{NB}\big(N_s \exp(x_s^\top \beta_g) + \rho_s T_s\,\mathrm{soup}_{gs}\big)$$

and tests $\beta_g$ with a quasi-likelihood F-test.

## A simulated study with known truth

`simulate_ambient_study()` makes 6 control and 6 disease samples. Cell type
`A` is abundant and has 80 disease genes. Cell type `R` is rare and has 40
disease genes of its own. Disease samples carry about 12% ambient RNA,
controls about 5%.

```{r simulate}
library(Decant)
st <- simulate_ambient_study(seed = 3, G = 600, n_cells = 500)
table(st$cond)
round(tapply(st$rho_true, st$cond, mean), 3)
```

Pseudobulk the rare type, one column per sample:

```{r pseudobulk}
is_R <- st$label == "R"
samples <- sort(unique(st$sample))
Y <- vapply(samples, function(s)
  rowSums(st$X[, is_R & st$sample == s, drop = FALSE]), numeric(nrow(st$X)))
rownames(Y) <- rownames(st$X)
dim(Y)
```

## Run the test

`empties` is a list with one empty-droplet matrix per sample, in the same
order as the columns of `Y`.

```{r test}
design <- model.matrix(~ st$cond)
res <- ambient_de(Y, st$empties, design)
head(res[, c("gene", "logFC", "PValue", "FDR", "ambient_frac", "naive_FDR", "ambient_driven")])
```

`naive_FDR` is standard edgeR on the same pseudobulk. `ambient_driven` marks
genes that edgeR calls and the contamination-aware test does not.

## Score against the truth

```{r score}
gi <- as.integer(sub("g", "", res$gene))
leaked <- gi %in% st$de_abund   # A's disease genes: any call in R is false
true_de <- gi %in% st$de_rare   # R's own disease genes
c(leaked_called_naive  = sum(res$naive_FDR[leaked] < 0.1),
  leaked_called_decant = sum(res$FDR[leaked] < 0.1),
  power_naive  = mean(res$naive_FDR[true_de] < 0.1),
  power_decant = mean(res$FDR[true_de] < 0.1))
```

The per-sample ambient fractions the test estimated:

```{r samples}
attr(res, "samples")
```

## On a Seurat object

`DecantDE()` does the pseudobulking and reads each donor's raw matrix:

```{r seurat, eval = FALSE}
res <- DecantDE(obj, cell_type = "Microglia", sample_col = "donor",
                formula = ~ diagnosis, raw = raw_paths_by_donor)
subset(res, ambient_driven)
```

## What this does not show

- The simulator is built around the additive-soup mechanism the test
  assumes. This vignette shows the method does what it is designed to do. It
  is not real-data evidence.
- Correcting counts first and then testing is not always worse. In
  `validation/de_comparators.R`, official SoupX followed by edgeR removes
  almost all leakage on this simulator, at some cost in power. See the
  README for the table.
- With very few empty droplets, or three samples per group, the test leaks
  or loses power. The README lists the measured limits.

sessionInfo()
